introduction: The readings of this guide speak of the Manifestation of God as a tree: the Tree of Life, the Bush that burned on Sinai, the Lote-Tree beyond which there is no passing, under whose shade people shelter and whose branches, leaves and fruits are told to hold fast. Beside them stand the older texts from which these figures come, the trees of Genesis, the Psalms and the prophets, the vine and the fruit of the Gospels, the tree and the lote-tree of the Qur’an, together with poets and teachers from other settings. Some question the figure: a law against sacred trees, a still small voice, a fable of trees choosing a king, a Great Law that plants a tree of peace of its own.
questions: What does the figure of a tree say about a Manifestation of God that the figures of sun, light or word do not?
The readings speak of a Tree that calls out. How do the older accounts of the bush and the mount help you hear that language, and where do they caution against it?
What is asked of those called fruits, leaves and branches, and how do the Gospel sayings about fruit sharpen the demand?
Where in these pages does shelter under the Tree mean rest, and where does it mean a duty?
Which quotation set in contrast changed how you read the passage it follows?

outside.why: Proverbs calls wisdom a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, an old use of the figure for something more than a plant.
John's vision promises the tree of life in the paradise of God to the one who overcomes.
A dream in Daniel shows a tree seen to the end of the earth, sheltering and feeding all, as this Tree shades East and West.
Ezekiel hears God promise a planted cedar in whose shadow birds of every wing shall dwell.
The psalm likens the righteous to a tree by the rivers that brings forth its fruit in season.
The law of Moses forbids planting any tree beside the altar of the Lord. What separates a holy tree used as a figure from a tree that is worshipped?
The Qur’an likens a goodly saying to a goodly tree, firm in root and reaching into heaven, as the reading joins Word and Tree.
This is the Bible's last picture of the tree of life, bearing fruit every month, its leaves for the healing of the nations.
The psalm promises that those planted in the house of the Lord still bear fruit in old age, as the branch here is green in every season.
In Exodus God calls from the midst of the bush and names the ground holy, as the reading summons people to a spot where the Tree speaks.
Exodus tells of the bush that burned and was not consumed, the sign the reading says people once accepted.
The Qur’an has Moses called from the tree in the blessed field, and the voice declares itself God, Lord of the Worlds.
Browning finds every common bush afire with God, for whoever sees. Is the Burning Bush one place and one day, or a way of seeing any place?
Asked who he is, John the Baptist calls himself only a voice crying in the wilderness, a speaker who points beyond himself.
Moses' last blessing has the Lord come from Sinai and shine forth from mount Paran with a fiery law in his right hand.
Deuteronomy warns that at Horeb the people saw no likeness, only heard speech from the fire, lest they make an image. How does that caution bear on language of a Face beheld at Sinai?
Isaiah foretells a rod from the stem of Jesse and a Branch growing out of his roots, a person spoken of as a branch.
Jeremiah too calls a coming king the righteous Branch raised unto David, who shall execute justice in the earth.
A chapter of the Qur’an opens by swearing by the fig, the olive and Mount Sinai together, trees and mountain side by side.
Job sees hope even for a tree cut down, that it will sprout again. What would make a tree deathless rather than merely hard to kill?
Jesus closes his sayings with this summons to whoever has ears, as the reading blesses the ear that has heard.
Rumi opens his great poem by bidding us hearken to a reed that speaks of its banishment from its home.
The exiled Duke finds tongues in trees and sermons in stones wherever he walks. Does all nature speak, or one Tree on one day?
Jesus says every plant his heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up; what matters about a tree is its Planter.
This single verse of the Qur’an is the source of the name the reading uses, the lote-tree of the utmost boundary.
Exodus describes Sinai on the third day with thunders, lightnings, a thick cloud and a trumpet exceeding loud.
The Light Verse speaks of a lamp kindled from a blessed olive tree neither of the East nor of the West, the phrase used here.
Shelley asks the wind to make him its lyre as the forest is, a tree stirred into sound by a breath.
The psalm has the children of men put their trust under the shadow of God's wings, as all might shelter beneath one leaf.
Isaiah pictures a man who is a covert from the tempest and the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.
Elijah, a day into the wilderness, sits under a juniper tree and asks to die. What turns a tree's shade from the end of a flight into an arrival?
The psalm promises that whoever dwells in the secret place of the Most High abides under the shadow of the Almighty.
The Song of Songs has the beloved as an apple tree among the trees of the wood, under whose shadow she sits with great delight.
Boaz honours Ruth, a stranger who left father, mother and native land to come among a people she had not known.
The psalmist's soul faints for the courts of the Lord, where even the sparrow has found a house and the swallow a nest.
The psalmist wishes for a dove's wings, to fly away and be at rest. Is repose found by flying from the world or by sitting down beneath something in it?
Jesus likens the kingdom to a seed that becomes a tree where the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches.
Kabir has God say he is beside the seeker, in neither temple nor mosque, Kaaba nor Kailash. Why then set one's face toward a station at all?
The psalm has all the trees of the wood rejoice with field, sea and heaven, a rustling that is itself praise.
Jesus says the Father will be worshipped neither on this mountain nor at Jerusalem, but in spirit and in truth. Does a Station to turn toward fit that saying or strain it?
Jesus tells his disciples he chose them to go and bring forth fruit that remains, as the Tree here raises up its own fruit.
Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness and temperance.
Jesus calls himself the vine and his followers the branches, fruitful only while they abide in him.
Jesus gives the test that the tree is known by its fruit, and that the mouth speaks from the heart's abundance.
In John the Father is glorified when the disciples bear much fruit, fruit borne for another's sake.
Marcus praises the one who does good like a vine bearing grapes and seeking nothing more. Should fruit know whose it is, or simply be borne?
Isaiah's song tells of a vineyard fenced, cleared and planted with the choicest vine by its owner. What can a well-planted tree still fail to give?
Jesus asks whether men gather grapes of thorns or figs of thistles; a claim to speak for God is tested by its fruit.
Luke gives the same rule, that a good tree does not bring forth corrupt fruit and each is known by its own.
Isaiah hears a voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord, a call addressed to a whole people.
A voice bids Isaiah cry out, and the first thing he is given to cry is that all flesh is grass.
Elijah's Lord was not in the fire, and after the fire came a still small voice. Must the divine call cry out amidst all beings in order to be heard?
Moses tells Israel that the Lord has not given them a heart to perceive or ears to hear unto that day. If hearing is itself given, how far can a summons to hearken be obeyed?
At the seventh trumpet great voices in heaven declare that the kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord.
Ezekiel sees trees growing on both banks of a river, unfading in leaf and bearing new fruit in their months.
James asks his readers to receive with meekness the engrafted word, speech pictured as a living graft.
Isaiah sees mountains break forth into singing and all the trees of the field clap their hands.
Jesus answers those who would silence his disciples that if they held their peace the very stones would cry out.
The Qur’an imagines every tree on earth a pen and the sea ink, and the words of God still unexhausted.
Genesis tells of the first garden, planted by God eastward in Eden with every tree pleasant to the sight.
The sower's seed bears richly only in good ground, and the parable ends by asking who has ears to hear.
Jesus tells Martha, troubled about many things, that one thing is needful and Mary has chosen that good part.
Noah's dove returns at evening with an olive leaf in her mouth, a bird and a leaf together bringing news.
At the baptism of Jesus the heavens open and he sees the Spirit of God descending like a dove.
Paul puts it in a line: faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Isaiah has God say, I have called thee by thy name, thou art mine: the comfort of being singled out and named.
The psalmist asks whom he has in heaven but God, and desires none upon earth beside him.
Zacchaeus, too small to see over the crowd, ran ahead and climbed a sycomore tree. What does hastening with the heart look like in the feet?
Jesus speaks of other sheep who shall hear his voice, until there is one fold and one shepherd.
Jesus calls his hearers blessed for what their eyes see and their ears hear, as the reading does those who heard in the days of God.
Hosea promises that Israel shall cast forth roots as Lebanon, and that they who dwell under his shadow shall return.
Jesus laments over Jerusalem that kills the prophets, whose children he would have gathered as a hen gathers her chickens under her wings.
Micah accuses priests who teach for hire and prophets who divine for money while saying the Lord is among them.
The Fathers trace the Torah from Moses at Sinai through Joshua, the elders and the prophets to the Men of the Great Assembly. Can a revelation reach later ages without the learned who hand it on?
The psalm recalls a vine brought out of Egypt and planted, taking deep root until its shadow covered the hills.
Jeremiah's tree planted by the waters spreads its roots by the river and does not see when heat comes.
In John every fruitless branch is taken away and every fruitful one is pruned. Is holding fast enough, or must a branch also bear and be cut?
Paul reminds branches grafted into the olive tree not to boast, for they do not bear the root but the root them.
Cyprian pictures unity as many branches of a tree with one strength in its root, and many rays with one light.
Confucius notes that only when the year grows cold do we learn that pine and cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
Luke records the women who went with Jesus through city and village as he preached the kingdom of God.
The psalm blesses a household, the wife as a fruitful vine and the children like olive plants round about the table.
Pope says education forms the mind just as a bent twig inclines the tree. Is a grafting done to a person, or something a person must take?

The Great Law of the Haudenosaunee plants a Tree of the Great Peace whose roots spread in four directions for other nations to follow. How should a reader weigh other peoples' trees beside the claim made here?
Jesus tells of a fig tree planted in a vineyard whose owner came seeking fruit on it and found none.
Thoreau says a thousand hack at the branches of evil for one who strikes at the root. Does looking to the root excuse what the leaves do, or explain it?
An Indian teacher points to the unseen essence within a fig seed, from which the great nyagrodha tree exists.
In Luke the good ground is those who hear the word, keep it and bring forth fruit with patience.
In Jotham's fable the olive, fig and vine decline to reign over the trees and only the bramble accepts, bidding them trust in its shadow. What does the fable warn about rank among trees?
A man planting a carob says in the Talmud that as his ancestors planted for him, he plants for his descendants.
Isaiah foresees the ears of the deaf unstopped and the tongue of the dumb singing, as the reading has the mute speak like a nightingale.
Jesus says the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man has not where to lay his head. Who shelters the one who is the shelter?
Isaiah promises mourners the oil of joy for mourning, that they might be called trees of righteousness.
The psalmist finds God already present wherever he might go, even on the wings of the morning.
The psalmist calls himself a green olive tree in the house of God, trusting in mercy for ever.
Hopkins sees the banks leaved thick again while he breeds no work that wakes. Can a prayer speak from barrenness as honestly as from verdure?
The Qur’an says that not a leaf falls but God knows it, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth.
The psalm calls fire and hail, mountains and hills, fruitful trees and all cedars to praise together.
Isaiah promises the fir tree instead of the thorn and the myrtle instead of the brier, an everlasting sign.
The psalmist saw the wicked spreading like a green bay tree, and then he was gone. How does the exaltation asked for here differ from flourishing that passes?

proverbs-tree-of-life-to-them.text: She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and happy is every one that retaineth her

daniel-tree-in-the-midst-of-the-earth.text: I saw, and behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was great. The tree grew, and was strong, and the height thereof reached unto heaven, and the sight thereof to the end of all the earth: The leaves thereof were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all: the beasts of the field had shadow under it, and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof, and all flesh was fed of it

ezekiel-fowl-of-every-wing.text: Thus saith the Lord God; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent: In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell

quran-lote-tree-of-the-utmost-boundary.text: By the lote-tree of the utmost boundary,

quran-from-the-tree-o-moses.text: And when he reached it, he was called from the right side of the valley in the blessed field, from the tree: O Moses! Lo! I, even I, am Allah, the Lord of the Worlds;

song-under-his-shadow.text: As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste

isaiah-shadow-of-a-great-rock.text: And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land

jeremiah-righteous-branch.text: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth

psalm-olive-plants.text: Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house: thy children like olive plants round about thy table

deuteronomy-not-plant-a-grove.text: Thou shalt not plant thee a grove of any trees near unto the altar of the Lord thy God, which thou shalt make thee

psalm-green-olive-tree.text: But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God: I trust in the mercy of God for ever and ever

judges-trees-went-forth.text: The trees went forth on a time to anoint a king over them; and they said unto the olive tree, Reign thou over us. But the olive tree said unto them, Should I leave my fatness, wherewith by me they honour God and man, and go to be promoted over the trees? And the trees said to the fig tree, Come thou, and reign over us. But the fig tree said unto them, Should I forsake my sweetness, and my good fruit, and go to be promoted over the trees? Then said the trees unto the vine, Come thou, and reign over us. And the vine said unto them, Should I leave my wine, which cheereth God and man, and go to be promoted over the trees? Then said all the trees unto the bramble, Come thou, and reign over us. And the bramble said unto the trees, If in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow: and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon
